doc.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: State of jazz and young players
summary: Young lions should play together rather than lead their own bands; Wynton encourages young people to play blues and swing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What’s your outlook on the state of jazz these days?

Well it’s kind of fragmented, the jazz situation. And I think, for instance, I think all the young, the supposed young lions, they should be playing with each other, instead of all having their own bands. When things were at the height, you know, the Miles Davis Sextet and the Miles Davis Quintet, it was Miles Davis and Coltrane, and Philly Joe and Red Garland and Paul Chambers. But nowadays, every one of those people would have their own band. And I don’t think that’s really a good thing. I think all these young people should be playing with each other and develop. Because that’s the only way they can develop. I think that’s one aspect of it. And I think the jazz situation is very healthy and we see a lot of kids at Lincoln Center, a lot of young people come to our rehearsals and they get involved, and Wynton encourages them to play, and when we go out and tour he goes to all the different schools. Sometimes we go with him, sometimes he goes by himself. But he does encourage young people to play instruments, play jazz, and to play blues and swing. And I think it’s very important too to play blues and swing.
Well blues has got to be a part of the jazz music. And I was interested in hearing the second set last night, that they opened up with a blues tune. And it was really nice, just to hear some wailing.
